5b(c).fact: Ants organize their colonies into distinct specialized chambers dedicated separately to sorting brood by growth stage, stockpiling provisions, and isolating refuse in graveyard middens to prevent disease.
5b(c).misconception: Ants excavate tunnels randomly and store eggs, larvae, food reserves, and colony waste together within the same open spaces.
5b(c).pamphlet_summary: Maintain a darkened glass or acrylic formicarium between viewing sessions to encourage ants to excavate visible tunnels against the perimeter. Identify the queen by her enlarged thorax and swollen gaster, and locate partitioned chambers dedicated separately to brood rearing, food storage, and waste disposal (p. 42).
5b(c).socratic_question: When examining an active ant farm, what physical traits allow you to distinguish the queen from the workers, and why do the ants separate their brood from their food stores?

5b(d).fact: Queen cells are distinctive vertical structures resembling textured peanut shells that hang downward from comb edges rather than flush horizontal hexagons.
5b(d).misconception: Queen bee cells look identical to standard hexagonal worker brood cells across the surface of the comb.
5b(d).pamphlet_summary: Use cool smoke to calm worker bees before carefully lifting frames by the top bars to inspect the brood pattern and locate the queen. Estimate capped brood coverage across the comb, count peanut-shaped vertical queen cells along the frame margins, and calculate stored honey volume by measuring the area of sealed wax honeycomb (p. 47).
5b(d).socratic_question: When inspecting a hive frame, how can you tell a queen cell apart from ordinary worker comb, and how do you estimate the amount of honey without unsealing every cell?
5b(d).topic_title: Beehive Comb Brood and Honey Assessment
